claim: The dorsal funiculus in the spinal cord relays somatosensory information to the brain.
source: The dorsal funiculus in the spinal cord relays somatosensory information to the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the dorsal funiculus, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The dorsal funiculus is made of T-shaped bifurcation of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory axons.
source: It is made of T-shaped bifurcation of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory axons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established anatomical knowledge about the structure of the dorsal funiculus.

claim: Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation.
source: Our previous study has shown that Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation, but loss of Slit does not affect all DRG axons.
evidence: This claim references a previous study by the authors, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of Slit does not affect all DRG axons.
source: Our previous study has shown that Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation, but loss of Slit does not affect all DRG axons.
evidence: This is stated based on previous findings from the authors' prior study.

claim: Mice lacking Ntn1 had axons escaping from the dorsal funiculus at the time of bifurcation.
source: Using wholemount staining with tissue clearing, we showed that mice lacking Ntn1 had axons escaping from the dorsal funiculus at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from wholemount staining and tissue clearing.

claim: The misprojecting axons in Ntn1 mutants come from DRG neurons.
source: Genetic labeling confirmed that these misprojecting axons come from DRG neurons.
evidence: This is confirmed by genetic labeling experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 did not affect bifurcation but rather altered turning angles.
source: Single axon analysis showed that loss of Ntn1 did not affect bifurcation but rather altered turning angles.
evidence: This is based on single axon analysis data presented in the study.

claim: Mice with triple deletion of Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2 have a completely disorganized dorsal funiculus.
source: To distinguish their guidance functions, we examined mice with triple deletion of Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2 and found a completely disorganized dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from triple mutant mice.

claim: Comparing mice with different genotypes revealed additive guidance errors, demonstrating the independent roles of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Comparing mice with different genotypes using immunolabeling and single axon tracing revealed additive guidance errors, demonstrating the independent roles of Ntn1 and Slit.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparative analysis of different genotypes using immunolabeling and single axon tracing data.

claim: The same defects were observed in embryos lacking the cognate receptors of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Moreover, the same defects were observed in embryos lacking their cognate receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from receptor knockout mice.

claim: Multi-factorial guidance mechanisms ensure proper formation of T-shaped bifurcation during spinal cord development.
source: These in vivo studies thus demonstrate the presence of multi-factorial guidance mechanisms that ensure proper formation of a common branched axonal structure during spinal cord development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the collective experimental data.

claim: DRG central projections bifurcate in the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ).
source: Upon reaching the dorsal spinal cord, they normally bifurcate in a location called the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ; Mirnics and Koerber, 1995; Ozaki and Snider, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The bifurcated branches extend in opposite directions along the rostrocaudal axis, generating T-shaped junctions.
source: The bifurcated branches appear to extend in opposite directions along the rostrocaudal axis, generating T-shaped junctions, as part of the dorsal funiculus in the DREZ (Figure 1E; Gibson and Ma, 2011; Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by both citations to previous literature and reference to Figure 1E in the manuscript.

claim: The dorsal funiculus is a critical axonal track in the spinal cord that allows information to flow between the PNS and CNS.
source: The dorsal funiculus is a critical axonal track in the spinal cord that allows information to flow between the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the function of the dorsal funiculus.

claim: Damage to or malformation of the dorsal funiculus can lead to paralysis.
source: Damage to or malformation of this evolutionarily conserved axonal structure in the DREZ can lead to paralysis, as commonly seen after spinal cord injury or in genetic disorders such as Frederick ataxia (Koeppen et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on spinal cord injury and genetic disorders.

claim: Ntn1 is expressed mainly confined to the inside of the spinal cord, including the floor plate, the ventricular zone, and the lateral domain in the dorsal horn adjacent to the DREZ.
source: Ntn1 transcripts are found mainly confined to the inside of the spinal cord, including the floor plate, the ventricular zone, and the lateral domain in the dorsal horn below the dorsal funiculus along the pial layer from E10.5 to E11.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B arrows).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In WT embryos, DRG central axons extend dorsally, enter the spinal cord, bundle and form the dorsal funiculus that runs along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: As shown in wild type (WT) embryos, the central DRG axons first extend dorsally, enter the spinal cord, bundle and form the dorsal funiculus that runs along the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wholemount staining data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, NF-labeled fibers escape the dorsal funiculus tract and fill the space above it.
source: However, while some axons remain in the tract, a subpopulation of NF-labeled fibers (Figure 1B arrows) were found to escape the tract, filling the space above the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is shown by wholemount staining data in Figure 1B.

claim: Misprojecting fibers appear in the hindlimb region where the dorsal funiculus starts to emerge, suggesting the defect happens at the time of bifurcation.
source: They appear in the hindlimb region where the dorsal funiculus starts to emerge (Figure 1D), suggesting that the defect happens at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of misprojections in the hindlimb region shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, an average of 22 fibers per DRG were found in the line proximal to the DREZ, 17 fibers/DRG in the medial line, and 14 fibers/DRG in the distal line.
source: In Ntn1β/β mutants, an average of 22 fibers per DRG were found in the line proximal to the DREZ, 17 fibers/DRG were found in the medial line, and 14 fibers/DRG were found in the distal line that is closest to the midline (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from line scan analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, NF-labeled fibers extended out from the DREZ at both E10.5 and E11.5.
source: However, in Ntn1β/β mutants, NF-labeled fibers extended out from the DREZ at both ages.
evidence: This is shown by transverse section analysis at E10.5 and E11.5.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 caused NF-labeled axons to escape from the DREZ.
source: Thus, loss of Ntn1 caused NF-labeled axons to escape from the DREZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed misprojections in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: tdTomato-labeled misprojections came directly from the DREZ in Ntn1β/β mutants.
source: Importantly, these tdTomato-labeled misprojections came directly from the DREZ (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by genetic labeling data in Figure 2C.

claim: All tdTomato-labeled misprojections are NF-positive in Ntn1β/β mutants.
source: While not all NF misprojections are tdTomato positive, all tdTomato-labeled misprojections are NF-positive (Figure 2B").
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-labeling analysis shown in Figure 2B".

claim: D2 dorsal interneurons are labeled by tdTomato staining but not by NF and thus do not contribute to the NF-labeled misprojections.
source: D2 dorsal interneurons inside the spinal cord are known to express Neurog1 (Helms and Johnson, 2003; Koundakjian et al., 2007). Although they are labeled by tdTomato staining, D2 interneurons are not labeled by NF (see Figure 2A and A") and thus do not contribute to the NF-labeled misprojections.
evidence: This is based on co-labeling analysis and citations to previous studies on D2 interneuron marker expression.

claim: In WT embryos, nearly all axonal terminals stayed within the DREZ.
source: For comparison, nearly all axonal terminals stayed within the DREZ of WT embryos (Figure 2I)
evidence: This is quantified from sparse labeling data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ~55% bifurcated and ~70% non-bifurcated axons in the Ntn1β/β mutants misprojected outside of the defined dorsal funiculus.
source: whereas ~55% bifurcated and ~70% non-bifurcated axons in the Ntn1β/β mutants misprojected outside of the defined dorsal funiculus (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is quantitative data from sparse labeling analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 alters the guidance of DRG axons at the DREZ during bifurcation.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of Ntn1 alters the guidance of DRG axons at the DREZ during bifurcation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single axon analysis data.

claim: Impaired Slit signaling led to misguidance of one of the bifurcated DRG branches, which enter the dorsal spinal cord in the absence of Slit/Robo signaling.
source: Our previous studies showed that impaired Slit signaling led to misguidance of one of the bifurcated DRG branches, which enter the dorsal spinal cord in the absence of Slit/Robo signaling (Ma and Tessier-Lavigne, 2007).
evidence: This is based on previous studies by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Misprojections in Ntn1 mutants appear on the dorsal pial surface and stay outside the spinal cord.
source: Since the misprojections in Ntn1 mutants appear on the dorsal pial surface and stay outside the spinal cord, we hypothesize that Ntn1 and Slit have different guidance functions that are both required for the formation of the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data and used to form a hypothesis.

claim: NF labeled axons are completely disorganized around the DREZ in triple mutants (Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β).
source: In contrast, NF labeled axons are completely disorganized around the DREZ (dotted-line region) in triple mutants (Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by wholemount staining data in Figure 3B.

claim: Both Slit and Ntn1 are needed for the formation and integrity of the dorsal funiculus.
source: This analysis of triple mutants demonstrates that both Slit and Ntn1 are needed for the formation and integrity of the dorsal funiculus and supports the notion that they have different guidance roles during DRG axon bifurcation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the triple mutant analysis.

claim: Slit and Ntn1 have different guidance roles during DRG axon bifurcation.
source: This analysis of triple mutants demonstrates that both Slit and Ntn1 are needed for the formation and integrity of the dorsal funiculus and supports the notion that they have different guidance roles during DRG axon bifurcation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of different mutant genotypes.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1+/+ double mutants, misprojections maintain a relatively straight trajectory perpendicular to the DREZ.
source: This can be demonstrated by viewing the misprojections from the dorsal side of the spinal cord (Figure 3K), as those misprojections maintain a relatively straight trajectory perpendicular to the DREZ.
evidence: This is observed from dorsal view imaging data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1+/+ mutants reach the midline but stop there without crossing to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
source: They also reach the midline but stop there without crossing to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is observed from the imaging data of Slit double mutants.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos, misprojections spread out in random directions from the DREZ along the dorsal spinal cord.
source: As in Ntn1 mutants, Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos have a large number of dorsal misprojections that spread out in random directions from the DREZ along the dorsal spinal cord when viewed from the side (Figure 3F, arrowheads).
evidence: This is shown by lateral view imaging data in Figure 3F.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β mutants are wavy and long, sometimes passing the midline and reaching to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
source: This can be corroborated by the dorsal view, which demonstrates that misprojections are wavy and long, sometimes passing the midline and reaching to the contralateral side of the spinal cord (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is shown by dorsal view imaging data in Figure 3L.

claim: The phenotype of triple mutants is more severe than that in Ntn1β/β mutants or Slit1;Slit2 double mutants.
source: As a result, the phenotype of triple mutants is more severe than that in Ntn1β/β mutants (Figure 1, Figure 3F) or Slit1;Slit2 double mutants (Figure 3E), which is demonstrated by an increase in these dorsally oriented fibers extending at all three proximal-medial-distal locations between the DREZ and the roof plate (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison of misprojections across genotypes shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Neither Ntn1 nor Slit is required for branch formation.
source: Since bifurcation remains nearly intact at this age for all these mutants, we conclude neither Ntn1 nor Slit is required for the formation of two branches.
evidence: This is concluded from DiI single axon labeling data showing that bifurcation occurs in all mutant genotypes.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutant embryos, 32 out of 34 axons analyzed have two branches.
source: In Ntn1β/β mutants, 32 out of 34 axons analyzed also have two branches (Figure 4F), indicating that branch formation itself is not affected in the absence of Ntn1.
evidence: This is quantitative data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos, 28 out of 29 axons have bifurcated.
source: Similarly, 28 out of 29 axons have bifurcated in the Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is quantitative data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In triple Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β mutants, 20 out of 21 labeled axons have two branches.
source: while 20 out of 21 labeled axons in the triple Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β mutants have two branches (Figure 4C and G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from DiI labeling shown in Figure 4C and G.

claim: In WT animals, the angle of bifurcation is on average 115.4°.
source: In WT animals, the angle of bifurcation is on average 115.4° (Figure 4H), consistent with a more curved trajectory of bifurcation at this age.
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos, the average angle is 118.9°, only marginally larger than WT.
source: When analyzed together, the average angle is 118.9°, only marginally larger than WT (Figure 4H)
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The angle deviation in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutants is increased to 19.5° and the angle difference to 31.6°.
source: but the angle deviation is increased to 19.5° and the angle difference to 31.6 ° (Figure 4I and J), reflecting misguidance of one of the two branches (Figure 4I) and consistent with the previous finding (Ma and Tessier-Lavigne, 2007).
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutant embryos, the average angle of bifurcation is ~108.0° with a deviation of 17.5° and a difference of 31.8°.
source: A similar angle difference was found in Ntn1β/β mutant embryos (Figure 4F). The average angle of bifurcation is ~108.0° (Figure 4H) with a deviation of 17.5° (Figure 4I) and a difference of 31.8°.
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4F, H, and I.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β triple mutants, nearly all branches are deviated from the average angle by a margin of 37.8°.
source: Although the average angle is 110.7°, similar to that of WT (Figure 4H), nearly all branches are deviated from the average angle by a margin of 37.8°, significantly different from that seen in either Slit1;Slit2 or Ntn1 mutants (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: The angle difference in triple mutants is increased dramatically, reaching 74.6°.
source: As a result, the angle difference is increased dramatically in the triple mutants, reaching 74.6° (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from angle measurements shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The guidance of the two branches has different requirements of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate the additive roles of Ntn1 and Slit, suggesting that the guidance of the two branches has different requirements of Ntn1 and Slit.
evidence: This is inferred from the angle analysis data showing additive defects in triple mutants.

claim: DCC was previously shown to have a late-ingrowth defect.
source: To further demonstrate the requirement of the two extracellular signals in guiding DRG sensory axons during bifurcation, we examined mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC, which was previously shown to have a late-ingrowth defect (Ding et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: DCC is expressed at low levels in the DRG by in situ analysis.
source: DCC is expressed at low levels in the DRG by in situ analysis (Faure et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: DCC is expressed in a subset of sensory neurons according to single cell RNAseq analysis.
source: and recent analysis by single cell RNAseq suggests DCC is expressed in a subset of sensory neurons (Faure et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a recent single cell RNAseq study.

claim: E10.5 Dcc mutants have similar misprojections as those in Ntn1 mutants.
source: Using wholemount analysis of E10.5 Dcc mutants, we found similar misprojections as those in Ntn1 mutants (Figure 5A and B, arrows).
evidence: This is shown by wholemount analysis data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Deletion of Slit receptors Robo1 and Robo2 results in the same overshooting error as the loss of Slit1 and Slit2.
source: Since the deletion of the Slit receptor Robo1 and Robo2 results in the same overshooting error as the loss of Slit1 and Slit2 (Ma and Tessier-Lavigne, 2007)
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Robo1-/-;Robo2-/-;Dcc-/- triple mutants show extensive dorsal misprojections that fail to form axonal bundles of the dorsal funiculus.
source: Fluorescent labeling of sensory axons in E10.5 wholemount embryos reveals extensive dorsal misprojections that fail to form axonal bundles of the dorsal funiculus in the triple mutant when compared with the littermate control (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescent labeling data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In Robo1-/-;Robo2-/- mutant embryos, the DREZ still forms but some fibers invade the spinal cord with straight trajectories that shoot horizontally in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: In Robo1-/-;Robo2--- mutant embryos (Figure 5G), , the DREZ still forms but some fibers invade the spinal cord with straight trajectories that shoot horizontally in the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 5I), similar to that in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- cross sections (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown by transverse section analysis in Figure 5G and I.

claim: In Dcc-/- only mutants, the DREZ still forms and the NF-labeled fibers misproject upward along the pial layer.
source: In Dcc-/- only mutants, the DREZ still forms and the NF-labeled fibers misproject upward along the pial layer (Figure 5F), leading to a reduced distance between the midline and the DREZ (Figure 5I), similar to the Ntn1 phenotype (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is shown by transverse section analysis in Figure 5F and I.

claim: In Robo1-/-;Robo2-/-;Dcc-/- triple mutants, two types of misprojecting fibers are found, similar to those in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β embryos.
source: In Robo1--/--;Robo2--/--;Dcc-/- triple mutants, two types of misprojecting fibers are found, similar to those in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β embryos (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown by transverse section analysis comparing receptor and ligand mutants.

claim: Loss of either the ligand or the receptor of both signaling systems has the same impact on DRG axon guidance at the DREZ.
source: These phenotypes are similar to those found in the analysis of Slit1;Slit2 and Ntn1 mutants above (Figure 3), thus demonstrating that loss of either the ligand or the receptor of both signaling systems has the same impact on DRG axon guidance at the DREZ.
evidence: This is concluded from comparative analysis of ligand and receptor mutants.

claim: Development of the T-shaped structure requires both Ntn1 and Slit, which regulate different aspects of guidance during bifurcation.
source: We show that development of this stereotyped T-shaped structure requires both Ntn1 and Slit, which regulate different aspects of guidance during bifurcation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: Multiple mechanisms ensure the proper formation of the dorsal funiculus, a structure that is essential to sensory function in the mammalian spinal cord.
source: These results demonstrate the presence of multiple mechanisms to ensure the proper formation of the dorsal funiculus, a structure that is essential to sensory function in the mammalian spinal cord (Light, 1988).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study findings and supported by citation to previous work on dorsal funiculus function.

claim: Ntn1 signaling is required for guiding bifurcating DRG axons in the DREZ.
source: Our analysis of mouse mutants lacking the secreted molecule Ntn1 expanded previous observation of a spinal cord ingrowth defect that was interpreted as the function of Ntn1 in a critical 'waiting period' before DRG axons sprout collateral branches (Watanabe et al., 2006). However, our study showed that loss of this molecular pathway also leads to a profound guidance error at the time of bifurcation
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings that expand on previous observations.

claim: Misprojecting axons were found as early as E10.5, when the dorsal funiculus first forms.
source: However, our study showed that loss of this molecular pathway also leads to a profound guidance error at the time of bifurcation, as misprojecting axons were found as early as E10.5, when the dorsal funiculus first forms (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ntn1 is needed for proper guidance of DRG afferents right at the time when they bifurcate in the DREZ.
source: The misprojecting axons do not stop at the DREZ but instead project more dorsally along the pial surface with random paths, supporting the idea that Ntn1 is needed for proper guidance of DRG afferents right at the time when they bifurcate in the DREZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of misprojection trajectories in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: Single axon labeling demonstrates the guidance role of Ntn1, which is different from what was suggested by previous studies.
source: Single axon labeling by both methods further demonstrates the guidance role of Ntn1, which is different from what was suggested by previous studies (Masuda et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on single axon labeling data and contrasts with previous interpretations.

claim: Previous studies suggested that Ntn1 blocks the DRG axons from entering the spinal cord when they initially arrive at the DREZ.
source: In these studies, DRG axons were found to enter from the ventral side of the DREZ in the medial spinal cord, leading to the proposal that Ntn1 blocks the DRG axons from entering the spinal cord when they initially arrive at the DREZ.
evidence: This is a summary of previous studies' interpretations.

claim: Ntn1 acts on bifurcating axons to guide their growth along the DREZ and loss of Ntn1 causes misprojections to exit the dorsal side of the DREZ.
source: Our data demonstrate that Ntn1 is required for guidance as well, but Ntn1 acts on bifurcating axons to guide their growth along the DREZ and loss of Ntn1 causes misprojections to exit the dorsal side of the DREZ (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Single axon DiI labeling at a later stage rules out the requirement of Ntn1 in bifurcation as the majority of DRG axons in Ntn1 mutants still form two branches.
source: Moreover, single axon DiI labeling at a later stage rules out the requirement of Ntn1 in bifurcation as the majority of DRG axons in Ntn1 mutants still form two branches (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both dorsal and medial misprojections were observed in recent studies of embryos with complete Ntrn1 deletion.
source: Interestingly, both dorsal and medial misprojections were observed in the recent studies of the embryo with complete Ntrn1 deletion (Moreno-Bravo et al., 2019; Varadarajan and Butler, 2017; Wu et al., 2019), suggesting that Ntn1 may play multiple guidance roles.
evidence: This is based on citations to recent studies.

claim: Ntn1 exerts its guidance function on DRG axons at the time of bifurcation.
source: Regardless, our single axon analysis (Figures 2 and 4) demonstrates that Ntn1 exerts its guidance function on DRG axons at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on single axon analysis data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The guidance function of Ntn1 is supported by the similar defect found in mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC.
source: The guidance function is further supported by the similar defect found in mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from DCC mutant mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: DCC function in DRG axons is reminiscent to that found in zebrafish DRG axons, which require proper DCC signaling to control actin-mediated invadopodia during the initial entry into the spinal cord.
source: This DCC function is reminiscent to that found in zebrafish DRG axons, which require proper DCC signaling to control actin-mediated invadopodia during the initial entry into the spinal cord (Kikel-Coury et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a zebrafish study.

claim: Ntn1 proteins present locally outside the DREZ may provide a permissive cue that encourages the growth of newly bifurcated branches but restricts their trajectory within the DREZ.
source: One is that Ntn1 proteins present locally outside the DREZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Serafini et al., 1996) provides a permissive cue that encourage the growth of newly bifurcated branches but restrict their trajectory within the DREZ, similar to the recently described role for Ntn1 in confining pontine neuron migration (Yung et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on Ntn1 expression data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The guidance function of Ntn1 may be mediated by a repulsive action of Ntn1, which can be mediated by both DCC and the repulsive receptor Unc5C.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that the guidance function is mediated by a repulsive action of Ntn1, which can be mediated by both DCC and the repulsive receptor Unc5C.
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism.

claim: Unc5C is expressed in DRG neurons.
source: This is supported by Unc5C expression in DRG neurons as well as the repulsive activity of Ntn1 on E11.5 and E13.5 DRG axons in vitro (Masuda et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is implied by the statement about Unc5C expression supporting the repulsive mechanism hypothesis, with citation to previous studies.

claim: Ntn1 has repulsive activity on E11.5 and E13.5 DRG axons in vitro.
source: This is supported by Unc5C expression in DRG neurons as well as the repulsive activity of Ntn1 on E11.5 and E13.5 DRG axons in vitro (Masuda et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Ntn1 signaling plays a key role in DRG axon guidance right after bifurcation at the DREZ.
source: Regardless, our studies demonstrate a key role for Ntn1 signaling in DRG axon guidance right after bifurcation at the DREZ.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: This is the first report of a severe defect of the dorsal funiculus where nearly all DRG axons leave the DREZ and grow medially into the dorsal spinal cord in triple mutants.
source: This is reflected by the severe sensory misprojections in triple mutants lacking all three genes, Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2, in which nearly all DRG axons leave the DREZ and grow medially into the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 3). Similar problems were found in mice lacking the receptors for both pathways (Figure 5). To our knowledge, this is the first report of such a severe defect of the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The guidance error found in Ntn1 mutants is different from that found in mice lacking Slit.
source: Importantly, when the misprojections were examined more carefully, we found that the guidance error found in Ntn1 mutants is different from that found in mice lacking Slit (Ma and Tessier-Lavigne, 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative analysis of misprojection trajectories.

claim: Misprojections due to the loss of Slit signaling tend to enter the spinal cord horizontally whereas those from the loss of Ntn1/DCC grow more dorsally and stay at the pial surface.
source: The misprojections due to the loss of Slit signaling tend to enter the spinal cord horizontally whereas those from the loss of Ntn1/DCC grow more dorsally and stay at the pial surface (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of misprojection trajectories shown in Figure 3.

claim: Misprojections in Slit/Robo mutants are relatively straight and horizontal whereas those in Ntn1 mutants are wavy and randomly oriented.
source: In addition, different growth trajectories were found for the misprojections: those in Slit/Robo mutants are relatively straight and horizontal whereas those in Ntn1 mutants are wavy and randomly oriented.
evidence: This is based on observation of misprojection trajectories in different mutants.

claim: Misprojections seen in Slit/Robo mutants enter the spinal cord from the middle or the dorsal side of the DREZ, which is different from those medial misprojections found in Ntn1 mutants.
source: It is worth noting that the misprojections seen in Slit/Robo mutants enter the spinal cord from the middle or the dorsal side of the DREZ, which is different from those medial misprojections found in Ntn1 mutants discussed above (Moreno-Bravo et al., 2019; Varadarajan and Butler, 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on observation and comparison with previous studies cited.

claim: Ntn1 and Slit have different actions in guiding DRG axons.
source: Nonetheless, these phenotypes suggest that Ntn1 and Slit have different actions in guiding DRG axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the different misprojection phenotypes observed.

claim: Loss of both pathways results in added defects for both horizontally and dorsally invading misprojections.
source: Quantitative analysis shows that loss of both pathways results in added defects for both horizontally and dorsally invading misprojections (Figures 3—5), suggesting non-redundant functions of the two mechanisms.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Slit and Ntn1 regulate branch guidance at two different steps during bifurcation.
